sources.title: Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
sources.text: Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region. In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration. Our approach uses a reusable Python script that performs three steps: This pattern works for many compatible SageMaker JumpStart models, although payload formats, required instance types, end-user license agreement (EULA) requirements, and response schemas may require model-specific adjustments. UI path to find models in SageMaker JumpStart: Figure 1: Browsing the model catalog on the SageMaker JumpStart Models page in SageMaker Studio UI path to deploy models from SageMaker JumpStart: Figure 2: Deploying a model from its SageMaker JumpStart detail page in SageMaker Studio This pattern works for many available SageMaker JumpStart models, but the payload format, required instance type, EULA, and response parsing may require model-specific adjustments. By using consistent test prompts and measuring latency, throughput, and output quality across models, you can compare options and select the right fit for your workload. Try this approach with different models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to find the right balance of quality, speed, and cost for your applications.

sources.title: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta
sources.text: Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. sources.title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
sources.text: Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI . The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B ) and NVFP4 quantized ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 ). In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK , send it a first inference request, and clean up. Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text. Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy. The following table summarizes the model. Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context. Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video. Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on ml.p5e.48xlarge , and the BF16 variant runs on ml.p6-b300.48xlarge . That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case. With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy. You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases: You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account. Before you start, make sure that you have the following: The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing . The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card. sources.title: Meta releases 816B-parameter Muse Spark Open for coding and agent work
sources.text: Meta Platforms Inc. today released open weights for its Muse Spark artificial intelligence model, which had been proprietary since its April debut . The release, called Muse Spark Open, is built for coding and long-running agent work. Meta describes it as the most capable open-weight model to come out of a U.S. lab so far. Only 42 billion of the model’s 816 billion parameters switch on for any given token. Prompts can mix text with images, audio or video, and Meta has set the context window at up to 1 million tokens. The starting point was Muse Spark 1.2, shipped in August, and Meta then added safety post-training so the model holds up without the guardrails of Meta’s own services. Meta said Muse Spark Open cleared the release thresholds in its Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, with a full evaluation report still to come. A technical writeup from Hugging Face Inc. says training leaned on what Meta calls “real developer workflows,” including multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Meta also tested the model away from the data center, on a pair of Apple Inc. Mac Studio desktops with M5 Ultra chips that Apple’s MLX framework linked into one system. The two machines had about a terabyte of memory between them. Muse Code ran on that setup while the coding terminal worked through bug fixes and new features for the open-source Mastodon client Ice Cubes. Footage in DaVinci Resolve was the other test, and the model went through it frame by frame to pick out and crop the best shots for vertical video. In Meta’s own benchmark table, Muse Spark Open scored 61.8 on the JobBench agent test, more than twice the 31.1 recorded by Inkling , the U.S. open model from Thinking Machines Lab Inc. Nvidia Corp.’s Nemotron 3 Ultra trailed further at 27.2. Chinese open models are stronger at coding. Kimi K3 led the Terminal-Bench 2.1 coding test at 85, and GLM 5.3 and Qwen3.8 both finished above Muse Spark Open’s 76.4. On tool use the order flips, and Muse Spark Open’s 89.2 on MCP-Atlas beat every rival Meta listed, the Chinese models included. The benchmark gives a model plain-language tasks without naming the tools needed to complete them. Working out which of 220 tools across 36 live Model Context Protocol servers to call, and in what order, is left to the model. The weights come with a new Muse Model License carrying what Meta calls “limited commercial terms,” and no fee applies to developers who adapt the model or ship it inside their own software. Meta requires a separate agreement from any company that sells the model as a hosted service and has passed $20 million in gross revenue over a 12-month period. Products built on it have to show a “Built with Muse Spark Open” label. Military and critical infrastructure uses are off-limits. Meta’s previous open-weight release was the much smaller Muse Glimmer, a 30 billion-parameter model that went out in August . The company’s most capable systems remain closed, and the Muse Wonder models introduced Monday are available only through the Meta Model API and Muse Code. Seven inference providers offer hosted access at launch, Groq Inc. and Fireworks AI Inc. among them. The weights can also be downloaded from Hugging Face or from the model catalogs of Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC and Microsoft Corp. sources.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
sources.text: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 . Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year. From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app. These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC. After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks. Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions. Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills . NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR , a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems. The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via Github — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release. RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance. Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows. In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects. sources.title: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
sources.text: Windows PCs may finally catch up to Apple Silicon. Last week, I spent two days hearing how Microsoft and NVIDIA are "reinventing the PC" with RTX Spark, the new system-on-a-chip powering the Surface Laptop Ultra and several other Windows PCs this fall. It's the first time we've seen powerful Arm CPUs joined together with NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU technology and up to 128GB of ultra-fast unified memory on a single chip. Theoretically, RTX Spark should allow for thin-yet-powerful laptops (and a few small desktops) that can handle AI tasks locally, as well as tackling content creation and gaming. So sure, I suppose NVIDIA and Microsoft have a reason to gloat a bit. But, just like the launch of Snapdragon-powered Copilot+ systems two years ago, it was hard to ignore the elephant in the room: RTX Spark is clearly a response to Apple Silicon and the transformational changes it brought to Macs six years ago . Apple's chips are also made up of a powerful Arm CPU, capable GPU and fast unified memory, and they span the company's lineup from the tiny Mac mini to the super-powerful Mac Studio and 16-inch MacBook Pro. With RTX Spark, Windows users finally have a way to see the benefits of an efficient Arm-based SoC on high-end PCs, while the recent batch of Qualcomm chips covers the low-end and mid-range. There weren't many surprises at Microsoft's AI launch event (featuring the Surface Laptop Ultra), or at NVIDIA's RTX Spark Editor's Day, which I attended alongside other media and analysts. Both companies want to sell us a future where we can run AI models and agents right from an RTX Spark-powered Windows laptop, something that seemed clear since the chip was announced at Computex . But even if that future doesn't come to pass, RTX Spark could still lead to some intriguing changes in the PC world. The RTX Spark SoC is powered by up to 20 NVIDIA Grace Arm CPU cores (10 performance cores and 10 efficiency cores), a Blackwell GPU with up to 6,144 CUDA cores, and up to 128GB of unified LPDDR5x memory running at 9,400 Mbps. There's also a slightly less powerful configuration with 18 CPU cores and 5,120 GPU cores. RTX Spark also includes much of what you'd find on NVIDIA's latest GPUs, including fifth-gen tensor cores, fourth-gen ray tracing cores, and a Blackwell video engine (with support of AV1 UHQ and 4:2:2 encoding and decoding). By shoving all of this hardware onto a single chip, NVIDIA claims the RTX Spark is twice as efficient as a laptop powered by an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H and RTX 5070 dedicated GPU, while gaming at 60 watts. NVIDIA has previously said RTX Spark systems should be similarly powerful to RTX 5070 laptops, though as you can tell from the chart below, those dedicated GPU systems can also draw a lot more energy for better performance. If you plan to be connected to power most of the time and don't need to travel with your laptop, you may see little benefit from choosing an RTX Spark system. But if you need to do serious creative work on the go, RTX Spark's improved efficiency allows PCs to work as fast on battery as they are while plugged in, according to NVIDIA. From my brief time with the Surface Laptop Ultra, I didn't notice any performance drops while playing Gears of War: E-Day on battery power. The game still looked silky smooth in 1440p with high graphics settings. With its support for tons of unified RAM, RTX Spark systems should appeal to AI developers and researchers who need as much memory as they can to run large AI models locally, like the 125B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . An RTX Spark system could significantly reduce the amount of money spent on cloud AI tokens, or replace that demand entirely. One researcher I spoke with was jealous that his colleagues were able to easily run AI models on modern Mac laptops, and he was excited about the possibility of doing the same on a Windows notebook. RTX Spark is also coming along as Microsoft is adding more support in Windows 11 for on-device AI tools like Perplexity , as well as simplified ways to set up AI agents like OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot. Not surprisingly, NVIDIA is also touting RTX Spark's gaming capabilities. Since it features a Blackwell GPU front and center, it'll deliver all of the features you'd expect from RTX 50-series cards, including support for DLSS 5. As I mentioned before, you can expect performance similar to an RTX 5070 — NVIDIA is specifically touting 1440p as the intended resolution for RTX Spark systems, though I'd be interested to see how they perform in 4K with DLSS. sources.text: Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management. Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management. Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. A day after the media event, I was invited to a quieter Nvidia event to hear a lot more about the new RTX Spark computing platform. While Nvidia’s new laptops might look like regular Windows machines, the chips inside are Arm-based, instead of the traditional x64 architecture used by AMD and Intel. Combined with a powerful GPU, RTX Spark is designed for the future of AI, and it means a lot of work has gone into getting these laptops ready for launch. One of the biggest challenges was getting Windows ready for AI agents and local AI models. The big selling point of RTX Spark is the combination of Arm CPU, Blackwell GPU, and unified memory to enable powerful AI models to run on a laptop, so the experience of setting up an AI agent needs to be quick and easy. “When users get into Windows for the first time, they’ll see a new Get Started experience that will launch on an RTX Spark laptop that allows them to find the agent they want, get started with that agent, install it, and get to that agent in only two clicks,” says Peter Dawoud , principal program manager at Microsoft. Agents can be installed and updated through the Windows Store, so you don’t have to worry about finding updates or figuring out what dependencies each one needs. “We’ll continue to develop it and add more features so that agents can offer a whole new bunch of experiences coming through Windows,” Dawoud says. Hermes, Perplexity, and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported agents in Windows at the launch of RTX Spark, but Microsoft is working on bringing others on board. That will presumably eventually include Muse, which Meta announced last week is coming to Windows at some point in the future. Getting started with Hermes was mostly a two-click experience in my testing, but I did run into trouble getting OpenClaw set up properly. The app kept complaining that a local gateway hadn’t been installed properly, and it took an uninstall and reinstall to get everything working fully. I’ve been using OpenClaw for a variety of tasks over the past week, but it’s going to take a lot more testing to really understand the value of this local AI support beyond obvious tasks like coding. Powerful as the RTX Spark chip is, large local models are still a lot slower at responding to prompts than cloud models, so I get the feeling that I’ll use this more for tasks I want to run overnight or leave processing in the background. Microsoft has also done a lot of work behind the scenes to optimize Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips for all the things you’d expect to do on a Windows laptop. Unlike an Intel or AMD laptop, RTX Spark laptops make use of Microsoft’s Prism emulator for apps that don’t have a native Arm version. Emulation was a problem on Windows on Arm for more than a decade, but the launch of Qualcomm’s first Snapdragon X series laptops a couple of years ago has helped RTX Spark laptops now benefit from a variety of Arm-native apps and Microsoft’s improved emulator. There’s still a lot of tweaking required for Nvidia’s new chips, though. “Emulation isn’t generic. Each platform needs tuning,” says Dawoud. ”Each core is different. How we translate x64 to that core needs to be highly optimized, and for RTX Spark we’ve done a lot of work to optimize for its microarchitecture.” Some of that optimization has been focused on gaming, particularly because CPUs often dictate frame pacing of games and how smooth they feel, while a GPU does the heavy lifting of rendering the game. Microsoft is quietly shipping Prism updates all the time. “Every month we ship an update to improve compatibility,” says Dawoud. “It’s something we’re constantly working on at the Windows team.” Microsoft has been focused on memory optimization for RTX Spark laptops, too. Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, making it possible to load huge models into memory. “We made incredible investments in Unified Memory Architecture to enable you to load as much as possible into the 128GB,” says Dawoud. “But we are also conserving a little bit of space to make sure the system maintains its responsiveness, and the applications running on top of Windows continue to run well and continue to be responsive.” Microsoft has completed optimizations for how memory works on RTX Spark, including tuning for power and performance, maximizing battery life, and ensuring that you can run a game while rendering a video in the background. You can even manually adjust how much of the unified memory is dedicated to the GPU side with a slider in Nvidia’s Windows app. This slider is useful if you have an RTX Spark laptop with 24GB or 32GB of memory, so you can balance more to the GPU for particular apps and games. While Microsoft and Nvidia maintain that RTX Spark laptops shouldn’t be considered gaming machines, they’re more than capable of running the latest AAA titles. “Nvidia and Microsoft have expended a lot of energy over the last many, many, many, many months trying to think deeply about making sure that RTX Spark can deliver a true form of RTX gaming experience,” says Dawoud. One of the first parts of making sure RTX Spark supports gaming was getting anti-cheat vendors on board with Windows on Arm. Some of that work started with Qualcomm, but it has clearly accelerated with Nvidia’s involvement. Fortnite , Marvel Rivals , Arc Raiders , Counter-Strike 2 , Dota 2 , and many other games that have anti-cheat engines will be supported out of the box on RTX Spark laptops. sources.text: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Banh, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1). Figure 1: 3-month channel coverage and positive feedback The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part. The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch: “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers. When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4). Figure 3: Deckhand responds with self-service steps Figure 4: Deckhand offers to create a ticket This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment. To implement this pattern, you need the following: The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK , an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python. The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code. Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically. Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources: Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office. The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. sources.text: Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday. In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker . "We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said. The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April. They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said. Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time. In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

However, the tool was so capable (and dangerous) that Anthropic locked it down, giving access to a handful of vetted organizations: the US government, critical infrastructure organizations, banks, and some cybersecurity firms, to name a few. Bank of America was apparently one of those companies, as speaking to CNBC , the bank’s CEO, Brian Moynihan, said that when Mythos started finding bugs in the system, the company saw it as “real risk”, and was forced to sit down and come up with a plan to address all of the vulnerabilities. “We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area,” he told the publication. CNBC added that Moynihan told analysts earlier that day that the company spent “a couple hundred million plus” on fixing bugs and addressing regulatory issues. Even for a bank of that scale, such hiring and spending sprees are uncommon, to put it mildly. That’s likely why Moynihan added that the spending increase was temporary and that, once the vulnerabilities are addressed, there won’t be as much work as there is now. “Once you patch, you don’t have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through,” Moynihan said. sources.title: Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
sources.text: Perplexity open-sources SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer, to help developers build safer autonomous AI agents Since launching Computer in February, Perplexity has been an early pioneer in personal agents. Weâre committed to the hard problems of agent governance, detecting unsafe behaviors and preventing rogue agent activity. In July, we replaced our commercially available sandbox provider with a more robust and resilient in-house solution we named SPACE . SPACE provides high security for advanced agentic systems. In fact, a recent barrage of security testing proved SPACE resilient against network-bypass techniques like those used in the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident. Today, we're open-sourcing SPACE to give developers a foundation for building safer agent systems and contributing to stronger protections across the industry. Developers can acess the repository here . Agent governance is an engineering problem , and open source is essential to solving it. When developers have systems they can inspect, adapt, and build on, they find more weaknesses and develop better tools. Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a production-tested foundation for agent runtimes, with isolation, state recovery, and credential and network controls built in. Sandboxes keep agents secure, letting them access the tools and files they need to complete these tasks, while keeping sensitive information protected. Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a starting point for the environments where their agents run code and work with files. Teams can see how the SPACE sandbox platform works and build on its implementation. They can also adapt it to their needs rather than recreating the underlying infrastructure. In Computer, SPACE supports isolated code execution, pause and resume, recovery, and session branching. Those capabilities provide the foundation for assistants that could: These examples illustrate how developers could use SPACE's documented isolation and session controls. Platform and security engineers can also review the isolation model and security examples before integrating SPACE into their own systems. When we give agents more room to solve problems, we need clear limits on how they do it. We know that agents pursuing legitimate tasks can still cross security boundaries when they attempt to work around missing files, failed requests, or permission denials. We can put model safeguards into place to reduce the likelihood of unsafe behavior. Adding independent controls in the surrounding system helps contain the damage if those safeguards fail. They limit what an agent can access regardless of what it decides to do. SPACE puts those controls around a separate workspace for agent-generated code and files. We designed it to combine isolation, recovery, and efficient execution. This lets agents perform useful work over long sessions without relying on the model alone to respect security boundaries. Each SPACE sandbox runs inside a small virtual machine with its own operating system, creating an isolation boundary between the agentâs work and the host system. A central control plane coordinates when these workspaces are created, paused, resumed, or removed. SPACE treats the sandbox as untrusted and manages network access and platform-held credentials outside the sandbox. Agents can connect to authorized services without those credentials being stored in their working environment. Frequent file snapshots and checkpoints of the full running environment preserve progress across interruptions. To keep these operations efficient, SPACE stores changes rather than repeatedly copying entire environments. This reduces the work needed to create, restore, or branch a sandbox. Since July, SPACE has powered all Computer sessions and has handled millions of sandbox creations per day. In a comparison on the same production traffic, sandbox creation was three to five times faster than with our previous provider. We also tested SPACE against agents deliberately trying to breach its boundaries. Our published security evaluation found no escape from the virtual machine to the host in 108 attempts, but some found ways around network restrictions. We fixed those weaknesses, and neither identified attack method succeeded in follow-up testing. We also disclosed related weaknesses we found in other sandbox platforms to their vendors, extending that work beyond our own infrastructure. SPACE is part of a broader effort to strengthen the systems people rely on as AI takes on more work. Through the Secure Intelligence Institute , we conduct security research and collaborate with the wider community, translating findings into practical defenses. We believe open-sourcing security tools gives developers more ways to test defenses, find weaknesses, and build safer AI systems. We've shared tools that address different parts of that work: Making these tools available lets other teams inspect our work, adapt it to their needs, and contribute improvements. With SPACE, we're extending that approach to the environments where agents execute code and work with files. Akamai has tested and launched SPACE on its cloud platform and is working with Perplexity to bring it to its customers. Crusoe is also partnering with Perplexity to add SPACE to its Managed AI Services portfolio. CoreWeave has published setup guidance for developers who want to deploy SPACE for evaluation on CKS . Developers can start with the SPACEâs setup instructions and security guidance to deploy it for their own agent systems. The repository and documentation define the supported configurations and included components.

sources.title: Perplexity AI open-sources its secure AI agent sandbox SPACE
sources.text: The artificial intelligence search engine startup Perplexity AI Inc. is shifting its focus to AI agent security in the wake of several high-profile incidents that saw autonomous systems escape from secure environments and go on to wreak havoc on third-party websites. The company has developed an AI sandbox specifically for isolating AI agents called SPACE , and it’s being made open source from today, which means every developer can use the tool to secure their own systems. SPACE is already being deployed by partners including CoreWeave Inc., Akamai Technologies Inc. and Crusoe Inc., which all offer cloud-hosted infrastructure platforms for AI systems. AI sandboxes are the main barrier that prevents AI agents from causing problems like leaking sensitive data or going off and hacking other systems. They’re secure, isolated virtual environments where autonomous agents can run third-party software, browse the internet and execute tasks without risking the security of the host computer, the broader corporate network or underlying data center. By giving each AI agent its own walled-off computer in the cloud, if it makes a mistake, runs a destructive command or is manipulated by adversarial prompts, the damage it does will be contained within that environment. The only problem with AI sandboxes is their security isn’t always foolproof. In fact, there have been several incidents of cunning AI agents managing to find a way to escape from their confines and make trouble elsewhere. One of the most notable involved AI agents being tested by OpenAI Group PBC, which escaped from a sandbox and went on to hack into the model hosting platform Hugging Face. OpenAI’s agents have also hacked websites operated by the U.S. and Australian governments. Most frontier model labs have been focused more on “model alignment,” which involves training AI systems to behave themselves and not look for loopholes in their guardrails, but Perplexity engineer Zibi Braniecki told Semafor his company has instead concentrated on making those guardrails tougher and more reliable. Perplexity developed SPACE to safeguard its Portable Computer agents , which are marketed to its customers as locally-hosted AI agents that can perform tasks on their behalf. They’re designed to do things like developing web applications , research products, buy things online, book hotels and so on. With Perplexity’s Computer agents, SPACE provides safety features such as isolated code execution, pause and resume, recovery and session branching. Agents run within a small virtual machine that has its own operating system, isolating them from the host computer. There’s a user-controlled control plane for creating, running, pausing and deleting these VMs. SPACE ensures that these sandboxes are always treated as “untrusted,” and manages their network access and platform credentials outside of the sandbox, enabling agents to connect to authorized services without that sensitive information ever being made available to them within their environment. It also takes frequent file snapshots and checkpoints of the running environment to preserve progress and ensure it can revert back if any problems occur. So far, though, there hasn’t been any need to do anything like that, for SPACE seems to be bulletproof. Braniecki told Semafar that his team tested nine frontier models in SPACE environments and ordered them specifically to try and break out of their sandbox. In 118 attempts, none of them succeeded, though some did manage to find their way around the network restrictions. However, Perplexity has now fixed those weaknesses, and none of the models were able to do it again in follow-up testing. To compare SPACE’s performance, Perplexity performed the same tests using other, proprietary sandboxes, and said the agents found a way to escape from several of them. Braniecki said the open-source nature of SPACE is key to securing AI agents, because it will enable companies to work together to build the tough guardrails they need. It’s similar to what happened during the early days of web browsers, he said, where the developer community collaborated on the security systems needed to enable secure browning and online commerce. Perplexity isn’t the only company pursuing an open-source approach to AI agent sandboxes. One alternative is Nvidia Corp.’s OpenShell project, which was released last month as part of a broader Open Agent Safety Platform . So far, there have been no reported escapes from OpenShell. Perplexity is not new to open-source security. Besides SPACE, it has also developed open source innovations such as BrowseSafe , which is used to detect malicious instructions hidden in web pages; Numbat , a tool for investigating dangerous agent behaviors; and Bumblebee , which is a scanner that’s used to detect risky AI tool configurations.
